For optimizing A* we usually look at the priority queue or the map representation. Often overlooked is improving the heuristic function. Here’s an example from the town of Denerim in Dragon Age Origins. Try moving the start and goal to see A* in action:

Now try moving the green to be near the purple . As the heuristic value gets closer to the true distance , the number of nodes A* has to explore decreases from to . The blue area is the savings.

On this page I’ll show a way to improve the heuristic to speed up A*. At the end of the page I show this technique with maps from real games.

 1  A*’s use of the heuristic#

A* uses a heuristic to guide it towards the goal. We can think of it like wind pushing us in the right direction. Here, the heuristic pushes us east, and the shortest path goes east:

But sometimes it pushes us in the wrong direction. Here, the shortest path is to the west but the heuristic pushes us east:

A* runs faster when the heuristic guides us in the right direction. It wastes time when the heuristic guides us in the wrong direction. But why is it in the wrong direction? It’s because the usual distance-based heuristic doesn’t know about the walls.

 2  Perfect heuristic#

Ideally, we’d find a heuristic that knows about walls and never points in the wrong direction:

Can we calculate this “perfect” heuristic? Yes!

But the perfect heuristic is different for every goal and wall configuration. Move the goal and you’ll see the heuristic changes. Move the start and you’ll see it doesn’t.

If the goal and walls stay the same, then we can use flow field pathfinding. But usually the goal isn’t the same, so we need to construct a brand new perfect heuristic for each goal. That is impractically slow to calculate every time we run A*, and it’s also impractically too large to store if we want to compute it ahead of time.

It’d be nice if we could calculate the heuristic once and then reuse it for multiple A* runs with different goals.

 3  Reusing a perfect heuristic#

Let’s calculate a perfect heuristic to the green landmark . Can we reuse it for another goal ? Yes, sometimes! Move the start point and the landmark around to see which purple goals are helped:

The idea is that if we already have the path from →, we also get the shortest path to any along the way:

And we almost have the path if the goal is near the path →:

But what does it mean to be “almost” the same? We can use the path length, cost(B, L). When the paths are almost the same, cost(B, L) is close to cost(B, X) + cost(X, L).

The A* heuristic is an estimated lower bound of the path length. For a heuristic we want a lower bound on cost(B, X). The triangle inequality[1] says that the sum of two sides of a triangle is at least as long as the third side. Adapted for directed graphs, we can say cost(B, X) + cost(X, L) ≥ cost(B, L). To calculate a lower bound, we rewrite this inequality as cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L) - cost(X, L).

That’s the key idea here. It’s impractical to precalculate all costs to all locations, but if we’ve precalculated the costs to a specific location , we can use that to estimate the cost to a different location .

 4  Multiple landmarks#

How often is this triangle inequality useful?

It depends on where landmark is in relation to start point and goal . We need to be “behind” when coming from . Move the start and goal around to see where a landmark would help:

Try moving the landmark outside the green shaded region, and see that the heuristic and path don’t always match.

Since a landmark needs to be “behind” the goal , a landmark won’t be useful for all goals. We need multiple landmarks L₁, L₂, L₃, etc. Each one gives us some lower bound for the heuristic: 

cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₁) - cost(X, L₁)
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₂) - cost(X, L₂)
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₃) - cost(X, L₃)
…
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, Lₙ) - cost(X, Lₙ)

We can take the max() of these to pick the highest bound. In this diagram, try moving the goal to one of the purple shaded areas to see how those areas are improved by the landmarks. Then try moving it to one of the unshaded areas to see how A* isn’t any faster there. Also try moving the start point to see how the shaded area also depends on where the start is.

 5  Placement of landmarks#

The best landmark position depends on the start point and goal . We want the landmark to be “behind” goal , but what’s “behind” depends on both where the start point is and where the goal are.

We want to use landmarks to improve as many (start, goal) pairs as possible.

Let’s start with a single landmark. Try moving the start point, goal, and landmark around in this map:

It looks like the landmark can cover the main corridors but not the side rooms. We need many more landmarks:

Picking the number and placement of landmarks is project specific. Consider:

  • Are all paths equally likely? For example in a colony builder game like Dwarf Fortress, we may care a lot more about paths to/from the main base, and not paths between a forest and a mine.
  • All all paths equally valuable to optimize? For example if pathfinding is limiting the frame rate, we might want to focus on long paths that are slower to compute and not on short paths.
  • Is the map static or does it change over time? If static, we might want to spend a lot of time in the map designer tool to precalculate optimal landmarks. But if dynamic, we might want to use the last few goal locations to decide new landmark positions. The new landmarks can be computed in a background thread.
    • If the change reduces an edge cost, the heuristic will overestimate sometimes, and A* will return a non-shortest path until we update the cost table. Pathfinding is optimized but nonoptimal. Example: the player broke a wall but the unit won’t look for the shorter path right away.
    • If the change increases an edge cost, the heuristic will be lower than desired, and A* will take a little longer to run until we update the cost table. Pathfinding is optimal but not optimized. Example: the player added a wall so the unit might think that area’s safe to walk through but will have to find a path around it.
  • If many units find paths to common areas (such as the Dwarf Fortress dining room), consider dropping the least used landmark and adding one near the common area.
  • Are the maps open world or constrained? A real time strategy game may have different needs than a room+corridor dungeon crawler.
  • Thomas Nobes has a video explanation[2] including more tips on where to place the landmark points.

Fortunately, even if a landmark isn’t optimal, it might still help somewhat, and it’s still no worse than if we use the regular A* heuristic.

 6  Automated placement#

One algorithm to place landmarks is to randomly generate paths and keep track of which locations are good for many different paths.

It usually but not always picks a spot in the upper left. It matches our intuition that landmarks should go on the outer edges of the map.

The second landmark should be away from the first landmark. The third landmark should be away from the first and second landmark. Each subsequent landmark should be evaluated based on what it adds. This is what it looks like with two existing landmarks:

It picks a third away from the first two, but not always in the same place.

 7  Implementation#

As the name “differential heuristics” suggests, this is a change to the heuristic given to A*. We don’t need to change A* itself.

We need to pick landmarks. If the maps are known ahead of time, landmarks can be placed in a map designer tool. If the maps are procedurally generated, try the randomized map analysis earlier on this page. Some of the papers linked at the end have more sophisticated placement algorithms.

Then we need to analyze the map. Allocate a 2D array of numbers, cost[nodeId][landmarkId].

For each landmark, we run Dijkstra’s Algorithm. It’s a “single source shortest path” algorithm but we want a single goal instead of a single source. In a directed graph, we need to reverse all the edges. In an undirected graph, we can use the edges as is. We set cost[nodeId][landmarkId] to the cost of the shortest path from node nodeId to node landmarkId. If the weights are all 1, we can use Breadth First Search instead of Dijkstra’s Algorithm.

This is essentially what I’m running for the demos on this page (undirected graphs): 

const L = [ /* array of landmark locations */ ];
let L_cost = [ /* array[nodeId] of arrays[landmarkId] */ ];
for (let landmarkId = 0; landmarkId < L.length; landmarkId++) {
    let output = dijkstraSearch(L[landmarkId]);
    for (let nodeId = 0; nodeId < graph.num_nodes; nodeId++) {
      L_cost[nodeId][landmarkId] = output.cost_so_far[nodeId];
    }
}

Note that it’s not much code. It’s running our existing algorithm (Dijkstra’s, A*, or BFS) and storing the results in an array. It could run in a background thread.

Then we need to modify the heuristic function. Previously the heuristic was distance(B, X). For example: 

function heuristicManhattan(a, z) {
    return Math.abs(a.x - z.x) + Math.abs(a.y - z.y);
}

Each landmark Li gives us a lower bound cost(Lᵢ, X) - cost(Lᵢ, B). We want to take the highest of these: 

function heuristicLandmark(B, X) {
    let h = heuristicManhattan(B, X); // or any base heuristic
    for (let i = 0; i < L.length; i++) {
        let lowerBound = L_cost[B][i] - L_cost[X][i];
        lowerBound = Math.abs(lowerBound); // if undirected
        if (lowerBound > h) { h = lowerBound; }
    }
    return h;
}

Note that it’s not much code. It’s running the existing heuristic (typically Manhattan, Chebyshev, or Euclidean distance) and sometimes increasing it if the landmarks form a good triangle.

What changes with the A* code? Nothing.

There are lots of techniques for making A* run faster. I like this one because it’s very little code.

 8  Demos#

I tried the differential heuristic on some maps from Dragon Age (provided by movingai.com[3]), a maze (also provided by movingai.com), and Cogmind[4] (maps provided by Josh Ge). All of these maps are undirected graphs (edges are bidirectional) so I’ve used that version of the differential heuristic.

  • Blue areas are what we no longer have to search by using the differential heuristic. Orange areas are what we search even with the improved heuristic.
  • Try moving the start and goal to see the performance on different paths.

 8.1 Dragon Age, The Circle Tower

The landmark is badly placed for the initial → path. Try moving it.

 8.2 Cogmind, Factory 5

In the next demo the landmarks are in places that don’t help. Move them around to improve search.

The blue area are the nodes we no longer have to search. More blue is better.

The landmark points help more when closer to the start point than the goal . They help more when they’re “past” the goal point. Move the start and goal around and see that there’s a big improvement no matter which path you want to find:

However, it took a lot of landmarks to get that improvement. We can do better by using the random path map analysis to pick fewer landmarks but in smarter locations:

 8.3 Maze

A* with a distance heuristic behaves particularly badly with mazes, but in this one, just four landmarks make a big difference! Then try clicking Random path repeatedly. The blue areas are the areas we didn’t have to search by using the landmarks. Also toggle the bidirectional flag to see how much of a difference that makes.

 8.4 Dragon Age, Lothering

This map has large open areas, and it seems to work well with the landmarks.

 8.5 Cogmind, Research 2

This is a room-and-corridor map from Cogmind.

 8.6 Cogmind, Factory 4

Another room-and-corridor map, common in traditional Roguelike dungeons.

 9  More reading#

This page is about using Cartesian coordinates in a game map to construct a graph-based heuristic based on “landmark” nodes (sometimes called “pivots” or “beacons”). I’ve collected some references but haven’t read all of them so I may have some of this wrong.

  • 2004 Computing the Shortest Path: A* Search Meets Graph Theory[5] (Goldberg, Harrison) [mirrors[6]]. I learned about the technique in this paper. It’s a combination of bidirectional A* search and the landmark-based heuristic, used for road networks.
  • 1994 Routing information organization to support scalable interdomain routing with heterogeneous path requirements (Hotz). [citations[7]] I can’t find a copy of this online, but it appears to be work that introduced using the triangle inequality with landmarks, for Internet routing.
  • 2005 Approximate Distance Oracles (Thorup, Zwick) [mirrors[8]]. This theory paper covers the more general topic of calculating the approximate distance between any pair of nodes in a graph, using a “distance oracle[9]”. An approximate distance is what we need as the heuristic in A*.

It’s also possible to go in reverse. Many graphs do not have natural Cartesian coordinates, and even the ones that do may not have good results from a distance-based heuristic.

  • 2002 Predicting Internet Network Distance with Coordinates-Based Approaches[10] (Ng, Zhang) [mirrors[11]] This paper uses the landmark-based heuristics to assign Cartesian coordinates for nodes in an Internet routing network. Then it uses Euclidean distance for the heuristic. This is the inverse of what we’re doing on this page, where we already have Cartesian coordinates, but want to use the landmark-based heuristic instead.
  • 2011 Euclidean Heuristic Optimization[12] (Rayner, Bowling, Sturvetant) transforms the Cartesian coordinates on a game map where distance heuristics don’t work well into new Cartesian coordinates where distance does work well.

Storing the landmark data requires one number per node. In a typical game map, those numbers may be very similar from one grid space to the next. Just as image compression takes advantage of nearby pixels having similar values, we might want to compress the landmark data because nearby graph nodes have similar values:

  • 2011 The Compressed Differential Heuristic[13] (Goldenberg, Sturvetant, Felner, Schaeffer) - by storing more landmarks in the same amount of space, the heuristic can be better. In this paper, “landmarks” are called “pivots”, and the “landmark based heuristic” is called the “differential heuristic”.

The landmarks L used on this page are placed beyond the end of the path B→X, so the layout is B→X→L. There are also algorithms that place landmarks along the path, B→L→L→L→X. I am not covering that topic here, but if you’re interested, see:

  • 2008 Approximating Shortest Paths using Landmarks[14] (Grant, Mould). Calls them “landmarks”.
  • 2014 Hub Labels: Theory and Practice[15] (Delling, Goldberg, Savchensko, Werneck). Calls them “hubs”, and uses only a single intermediary on the path B→L→X.
  • 2009 Abstraction-Based Heuristics with True Distance Computations[16] (Felner, Barer, Sturvetant, Schaeffer). I believe this paper tries to unify both “landmark” approaches. B→X→L is called “differential heuristic” and B→L→L→L→X is called “canonical heuristic”, and both of these are under the umbrella “true distance heuristics”.

I learned about this technique a long time ago, then tried writing it up in 2015. I realized that I didn’t understand it enough to be able to explain it. I studied it off and on in 2016, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2024, and 2026. I abandoned and restarted this page many times. And by 2026 I think I understand it well enough to write this page. However I haven’t used it in a real project yet.

Calls them “landmarks”. 2014 Hub Labels: Theory and Practice[15] (Delling, Goldberg, Savchensko, Werneck). Calls them “hubs”, and uses only a single intermediary on the path B→L→X. 2009 Abstraction-Based Heuristics with True Distance Computations[16] (Felner, Barer, Sturvetant, Schaeffer). I believe this paper tries to unify both “landmark” approaches. B→X→L is called “differential heuristic” and B→L→L→L→X is called “canonical heuristic”, and both of these are under the umbrella “true distance heuristics”. I learned about this technique a long time ago, then tried writing it up in 2015. I realized that I didn’t understand it enough to be able to explain it. I studied it off and on in 2016, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2024, and 2026. I abandoned and restarted this page many times. And by 2026 I think I understand it well enough to write this page. However I haven’t used it in a real project yet.

为了优化 A*，我们通常查看优先级队列或映射表示。 经常被忽视的是改进启发式功能。 这是《龙腾世纪：起源》中丹尼姆镇的一个例子。 尝试移动起点 B 和目标以查看 A* 的实际效果：

现在尝试将绿色 L 移动到紫色附近。 随着启发式值越来越接近真实距离 ，A* 必须探索的节点数量从 减少到 。 蓝色区域是储蓄。

在本页中，我将展示一种改进启发式方法以加速 A* 的方法。 在页面的末尾，我用真实游戏中的地图展示了这种技术。

1 A* 对启发式的使用#

A* 使用启发式方法来引导其实现目标。 我们可以把它想象成风把我们推向正确的方向。 在这里，启发式将我们推向东方，最短路径向东：

但有时它会把我们推向错误的方向。 在这里，最短的路径是向西，但启发式将我们推向东：

当启发式引导我们朝正确的方向前进时，A* 运行得更快。 当启发式将我们引向错误的方向时，就会浪费时间。 但为什么方向不对呢？ 这是因为通常的基于距离的启发式方法不了解墙壁。

2 完美启发式#

理想情况下，我们会找到一个了解墙壁并且永远不会指向错误方向的启发式：

我们可以计算出这个“完美”的启发式吗？ 是的！

但对于每个目标和墙体配置来说，完美的启发式都是不同的。 移动目标，你就会看到启发式的变化。 移动开头 B，你会发现它没有。

如果目标和墙壁保持不变，那么我们可以使用流场寻路。 但通常目标是不一样的，所以我们需要为每个目标构建一个全新的完美启发式。 每次运行 A* 时计算速度都太慢，而且如果我们想提前计算它，它也太大而无法存储，这是不切实际的。

如果我们可以计算启发式一次，然后将其重复用于具有不同目标的多次 A* 运行，那就太好了。

3 重用完美启发式#

让我们计算一下绿色地标 L 的完美启发式。 我们可以将其重新用于另一个目标吗？ 是的，有时！ 移动起点 B 和地标 L 来查看哪些紫色目标受到帮助：

这个想法是，如果我们已经有了从 B→L 的路径，我们也会得到到沿途任何路径的最短路径：

如果目标靠近路径 B→L，我们就几乎得到了路径：

但“几乎”相同是什么意思呢？ 我们可以使用路径长度，成本（B，L）。 当路径几乎相同时，cost(B,L)接近cost(B,X)+cost(X,L)。

A* 启发式是路径长度的估计下限。 对于启发式，我们需要成本（B，X）的下限。 三角形不等式[1]表示三角形的两条边之和至少与第三条边一样长。 适用于有向图，我们可以说 cost(B, X) + cost(X, L) ≥ cost(B, L)。 为了计算下限，我们将这个不等式重写为 cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L) - cost(X, L)。

这就是这里的关键思想。 预先计算所有位置的所有成本是不切实际的，但如果我们预先计算了特定位置 L 的成本，我们可以用它来估计不同位置的成本。

4 多个地标#

这个三角不等式有用的频率是多少？

这取决于地标 L 相对于起点 B 和目标的位置。 当来自 B 时，我们需要 L 在“后面”。 移动起点 B 和目标，看看地标在哪里会有帮助：

尝试将地标 L 移到绿色阴影区域之外，您会发现启发式和路径并不总是匹配。

由于地标需要位于目标“后面”，因此地标不会对所有目标都有用。 我们需要多个地标 L₁、L2、L₃ 等。每个地标都为我们提供了启发式的一些下限：

cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₁) - cost(X, L₁)
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₂) - cost(X, L₂)
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, L₃) - cost(X, L₃)
…
cost(B, X) ≥ cost(B, Lₙ) - cost(X, Lₙ)

我们可以使用 max() 来选择最高界限。 在此图中，尝试将目标移动到紫色阴影区域之一，以查看地标如何改善这些区域。 然后尝试将其移动到非阴影区域之一，看看 A* 在那里是否更快。 还可以尝试移动起点 B，看看阴影区域如何取决于起点的位置。

5 地标的放置#

最佳地标位置取决于起点 B 和目标 。 我们希望地标位于目标“后面”，但“后面”的内容取决于起点 B 的位置和目标的位置。

我们希望使用地标来改进尽可能多的（开始，目标）对。

让我们从一个地标开始。 尝试在此地图中移动起点、目标和地标：

看起来地标可以覆盖主走廊，但不能覆盖侧室。 我们需要更多的地标：

地标的数量和位置的选择是根据项目而定的。 考虑：

  • 所有路径的可能性均等吗？ 例如，在像《矮人要塞》这样的殖民地建设者游戏中，我们可能更关心往返于主基地的路径，而不是森林和矿井之间的路径。
  • 所有路径都同样具有优化价值吗？ 例如，如果寻路限制了帧速率，我们可能希望关注计算速度较慢的长路径，而不是短路径。
  • 地图是静态的还是随时间变化？ 如果是静态的，我们可能需要在地图设计器工具中花费大量时间来预先计算最佳地标。 但如果是动态的，我们可能希望使用最后几个目标位置来决定新的地标位置。 新的地标可以在后台线程中计算。 如果更改减少了边成本，则启发式有时会高估，并且 A* 将返回非最短路径，直到我们更新成本表。 寻路已优化但不是最优的。 示例：玩家打破了墙壁，但单位不会立即寻找更短的路径。 如果更改增加了边缘成本，则启发式将低于预期，并且 A* 将需要更长的时间才能运行，直到我们更新成本表。 寻路是最优的，但还没有优化。 示例：玩家添加了一堵墙，因此该单位可能会认为该区域可以安全行走，但必须找到绕过它的路径。
  • 如果许多单位都找到通往公共区域（例如矮人要塞餐厅）的路径，请考虑放弃最不使用的地标并在公共区域附近添加一个。
  • 地图是开放世界还是受限世界？ 实时策略游戏可能与房间+走廊地牢探索游戏有不同的需求。
  • Thomas Nobes 有一个视频解释[2]，其中包括有关在何处放置地标点的更多提示。

幸运的是，即使地标不是最佳的，它仍然可能有所帮助，而且仍然不比我们使用常规的 A* 启发式更糟糕。

6 自动放置#

放置地标的一种算法是随机生成路径并跟踪哪些位置适合许多不同的路径。

它通常但并不总是在左上角选择一个位置。 它符合我们的直觉，即地标应该位于地图的外边缘。

第二个地标应远离第一个地标。 第三个地标应远离第一个和第二个地标。 每个后续地标应根据其添加的内容进行评估。 这是两个现有地标的样子：

它从前两个中选择第三个，但并不总是在同一个地方。

7 实施#

正如“微分启发式”这个名称所暗示的，这是对 A* 启发式的更改。 我们不需要改变 A* 本身。

我们需要选择地标。 如果提前知道地图，则可以将地标放置在地图设计器工具中。 如果地图是按程序生成的，请尝试本页前面的随机地图分析。 最后链接的一些论文具有更复杂的放置算法。

然后我们需要分析地图。 分配一个二维数字数组，cost[nodeId][landmarkId]。

对于每个地标，我们运行 Dijkstra 算法。 这是一种“单源最短路径”算法，但我们想要单一目标而不是单一源。 在有向图中，我们需要反转所有边。 在无向图中，我们可以按原样使用边。 我们将cost[nodeId][landmarkId]设置为从节点nodeId到节点landmarkId的最短路径的成本。 如果权重都为1，我们可以使用广度优先搜索代替Dijkstra算法。

这基本上就是我在本页上运行的演示（无向图）：

const L = [ /* array of landmark locations */ ];
let L_cost = [ /* array[nodeId] of arrays[landmarkId] */ ];
for (let landmarkId = 0; landmarkId < L.length; landmarkId++) {
    let output = dijkstraSearch(L[landmarkId]);
    for (let nodeId = 0; nodeId < graph.num_nodes; nodeId++) {
      L_cost[nodeId][landmarkId] = output.cost_so_far[nodeId];
    }
}

请注意，代码不多。 它运行我们现有的算法（Dijkstra、A* 或 BFS）并将结果存储在数组中。 它可以在后台线程中运行。

然后我们需要修改启发式函数。 以前的启发式是距离(B, X)。 例如：

function heuristicManhattan(a, z) {
    return Math.abs(a.x - z.x) + Math.abs(a.y - z.y);
}

每个地标 Li 都给我们一个下限成本(Lᵢ, X) - 成本(Lᵢ, B)。 我们想取其中最高的：

function heuristicLandmark(B, X) {
    let h = heuristicManhattan(B, X); // or any base heuristic
    for (let i = 0; i < L.length; i++) {
        let lowerBound = L_cost[B][i] - L_cost[X][i];
        lowerBound = Math.abs(lowerBound); // if undirected
        if (lowerBound > h) { h = lowerBound; }
    }
    return h;
}

请注意，代码不多。 它运行现有的启发式（通常是曼哈顿距离、切比雪夫距离或欧几里得距离），如果地标形成一个好的三角形，有时会增加启发式。

A* 代码有何变化？ 没有什么。

有很多技术可以让 A* 运行得更快。 我喜欢这个，因为它的代码很少。

9 更多阅读#

本页介绍的是在游戏地图中使用笛卡尔坐标来构建基于“地标”节点（有时称为“枢轴”或“信标”）的基于图形的启发式方法。 我收集了一些参考资料，但没有阅读全部，所以我可能有一些错误。

  • 2004 年计算最短路径：A* 搜索遇见图论[5]（Goldberg、Harrison）[mirrors[6]]。 我在这篇论文中了解了该技术。 它结合了双向 A* 搜索和基于地标的启发式算法，用于道路网络。
  • 1994 路由信息组织支持具有异构路径要求的可扩展域间路由 (Hotz)。 [引用[7]] 我在网上找不到这个副本，但它似乎是介绍使用带有地标的三角不等式进行互联网路由的工作。
  • 2005 年近似距离预言（Thorup、Zwick）[镜子[8]]。 这篇理论论文涵盖了使用“距离预言机[9]”计算图中任意一对节点之间的近似距离的更一般主题。 我们需要一个近似距离作为 A* 中的启发式。

反过来也是可以的。 许多图没有自然的笛卡尔坐标，即使有，基于距离的启发式也可能不会得到好的结果。

  • 2002 使用基于坐标的方法预测互联网网络距离[10]（Ng，Zhang）[镜像[11]] 本文使用基于地标的启发式方法为互联网路由网络中的节点分配笛卡尔坐标。 然后它使用欧几里得距离进行启发式。 这与我们在此页面上所做的相反，我们已经有了笛卡尔坐标，但希望使用基于地标的启发式方法。
  • 2011 欧几里得启发式优化[12]（Rayner、Bowling、Sturvetant）将游戏地图上距离启发式效果不佳的笛卡尔坐标转换为距离启发式效果良好的新笛卡尔坐标。

存储地标数据需要每个节点一个数字。 在典型的游戏地图中，这些数字可能从一个网格空间到下一个网格空间都非常相似。 正如图像压缩利用具有相似值的附近像素一样，我们可能希望压缩地标数据，因为附近的图节点具有相似的值：

  • 2011 The Compressed Differential Heuristic[13] (Goldenberg, Sturvetant, Felner, Schaeffer) - 通过在相同的空间中存储更多的地标，启发式可以更好。 在本文中，“地标”被称为“枢轴”，“基于地标的启发式”被称为“差异启发式”。

本页使用的地标L放置在路径B→X的末端之外，因此布局为B→X→L。 还有沿着路径 B→L→L→L→X 放置地标的算法。 我不会在这里讨论这个主题，但如果您有兴趣，请参阅：

  • 2008 使用地标近似最短路径[14]（Grant，Mould）。 称它们为“地标”。
  • 2014 年中心标签：理论与实践[15]（Delling、Goldberg、Savchensko、Werneck）。 将它们称为“集线器”，并且在路径 B→L→X 上仅使用单个中介。
  • 2009 年基于抽象的启发式真实距离计算[16]（Felner、Barer、Sturvetant、Schaeffer）。 我相信本文试图统一这两种“里程碑式”的方法。 B→X→L 称为“微分启发式”，B→L→L→L→X 称为“规范启发式”，这两者都属于“真实距离启发式”。

我很早以前就了解了这项技术，然后在 2015 年尝试将其写下来。 我意识到我对它的理解还不够，无法解释它。 我在2016年、2018年、2019年、2022年、2024年和2026年断断续续地研究过它。 我多次放弃并重新启动此页面。 到 2026 年，我想我已经足够理解它了，可以写这篇文章了。 不过我还没有在实际项目中使用过。
